Travelers! From the _west_? Through the wold? Nobody comes through the wold. The wold doesn\'t let them.

So was the miller\'s flour. So were Tobble\'s honey-jars. Tam has all of it now.
...Is that girl all right? She\'s staring at her own hand.

A Crest? At her age? Oh, you\'ll want Old Bethan for that. The cottage up the hill, past the beehives. She knows Crests better than any priest.
The Choir threw her out for it, mind. Called her a heretic. _We_ call her "the Crestless Sage", on account of she\'s got about six of the things.
I\'d not say that to her face, dear. She boxes.
Visit the Crestless Sage in the cottage on the hill, north-east of Thistledown\'s green.

Door was open, so you came in. That\'s either brave or rude. Sit. Both is fine.
Are you— the Reeve said you\'re the Crestless Sage?
The Choir called me that. "The Crestless." Meant it as an insult, the dear things. Name\'s Bethan.

That— that\'s not possible. One Crest, one life.
Mender at sixteen. Arcanist at twenty-two, when I got bored of bandages. Ranger at thirty. Cantor at forty, to annoy a bishop.

He was wrong. I showed him how wrong. Twice.

_(quietly)_ The light knew I\'d be a Mender. I always knew I would be.
Course you did, herb-girl. That\'s your loudest thing. Doesn\'t mean it\'s your _only_ thing.
And you. Come here, child. Give me that hand.
Sixty years I\'ve been reading Crests. I\'ve never seen this one. Never read of it, neither — and I\'ve read everything the Choir ever tried to burn.
It\'s _yours_. That\'s all a Crest ever is. ...Cold, though. Like a hand that\'s been in the sea.
Whatever made this made it carefully. Mind that.
Right. Lesson. Do you want to learn to braid your Crests, or not?
Then show me what you\'ve got. Outside. I\'ll go easy.
Ha! Not bad. Not bad at all. You hit like a Dawnguard squire. Which one of you\'s the Dawnguard squire? ...Ah. That explains a great deal.
Up you get. No shame losing to an old woman. I\'ve had sixty years\' more practice at being difficult.
Did you watch? Every few breaths I was something different. Mender. Arcanist. Pugilist. Same old woman. Different _tools_.
Now hold out your hands. All of you. No, the Dawnguard boy too. Don\'t sulk.
She presses her thumb to each Crest in turn and hums a note so low you feel it in your teeth.
Your Crest grows warm. Then, for an instant, it feels like a door you never noticed — standing open.
The art of the *Braided Calling* is learned! Crests can now be changed freely, and advanced *Braided* Crests can be earned.
Here\'s how it works. I\'ll say it once, because I\'m old and you\'re young and one of us has to save breath.
Your *Primary* Crest is what you are today. It shapes your body — strength, speed, how much light can pour through you — and which weapons sit right in your hand.
Your *Secondary* Crest is what you\'re learning on the side. You can use its Arts in a fight, but it won\'t change your bones.
Every Crest grows on its own as you fight with it. Each rank teaches you an Art — or a *Support*. A habit. A knack.

And here\'s the bit the Choir hates: a Support you\'ve learned is yours forever. Learn to counter as a Pugilist and you\'ll still counter as a Mender. Your *Support Points* decide how many knacks you can carry.
Raise two Crests to rank five and they\'ll braid into something new. I won\'t spoil it. Experiment.
And a gift. Cantor — the singer\'s Crest. Songs that steady the heart. I learned it at forty to annoy that bishop. It\'ll suit at least one of you.
Pedrick at the trading post sells Crest Stones — bits of old Lantern-glass that remember a calling. Dear. Worth it.
Bethan... why did the Choir really throw you out?
I taught a boy, once. In Aurenne. A Keeper\'s son. Clever, sad thing — he\'d lost someone young, and couldn\'t bear to be helpless ever again.
He learned every Crest I could give him, and wanted more. The Choir said I\'d made a monster. I said I\'d made a boy who could _do_ things.
...I\'ve wondered since which of us was right.
He grew up. That\'s what happens to boys. Mostly.
Now. You\'ll want the Aurenne road, and that fool Tam\'s sitting on it. He used to steal my apples when he was eight. He was bad at it then, too.
His lads watch the quarry track. But there\'s an herb path behind the hedge at the far east end of the fields — up the hill to the quarry\'s back door. I\'ve used it forty years.
Tam doesn\'t know it\'s there, because Tam has never once in his life picked an herb. I\'ll have Corporal Fen pull the hedge back for you.
Take the Sage\'s herb path (behind the hedge at the east end of the fields) up to Red Tam\'s quarry.

Bethan, the Crestless Sage, has FIVE Crests. She says "one Crest, one life" is a lie, and taught us to braid our Crests. She once taught a Keeper\'s son who lost someone young. She wonders if she made a monster.
Told you Tam was bad at it.
Go on to Aurenne. And when somebody in a fine robe tells you what you are — you remember an old woman with five Crests and a bad hip.
Back already? Pedrick sells Crest Stones. Try a few on. Wear them like hats.
Herb path\'s behind the hedge at the east end of the fields. Mind Tam\'s archers.
Ask Bethan for another sparring match?
Fields are quiet. Crows are back. I\'ve never been so glad to see crows.
Stuffing \'em with honest straw from now on. Honest straw never walked anywhere.
Don\'t go in the fields. I mean it. Not the north field, not the south field, not the field I haven\'t named yet.
Scarecrows. _My_ scarecrows. They\'ve started... walking. At night, first. Now in the day, which is worse, because I can see them doing it.
Bought new stuffing for \'em off some lads on the road. Two silver a sack. Purple, it was. Glittery. Swore it\'d keep the crows off for good.
Like the crystal in the tide caves. The cold one.
Three of \'em out there. If you\'re the fighting sort — and you\'ve the look — knock \'em down for me. Leave Old Strawman for last; he was my granddad\'s, and he\'s _big_.
Farmer Dunstan\'s scarecrows have come alive after he stuffed them with cheap purple "stuffing". Put down the three in the east fields — Old Strawman last.
A scarecrow in a battered hat. Its button eyes seem to follow you. That\'s just a thing people say about scarecrows.\n...Isn\'t it?
This one is bigger. Older. Its stitched head is turned toward the other scarecrows, as if it is waiting to see what happens to them.
Old Strawman\'s head turns. Its friends are gone, and it has noticed.
The scarecrow\'s head turns. Slowly. Its stitched mouth splits into a grin full of violet dust.
There was a voice in the straw. Very small. It said "shoo." Over and over. "Shoo."
All three scarecrows are down. Tell Farmer Dunstan his fields are safe.
All three? Even Old Strawman? ...Granddad would\'ve hated that. He\'d also have hated a walking scarecrow, so. Swings and roundabouts.
Here. Take one of the horseshoes off the door. I\'ve three. Clearly they weren\'t working.
Dunstan — the lads who sold you that stuffing. Where did they say it came from?
Didn\'t say. Didn\'t have to. They came down the quarry track with it. Tam\'s lot, the thieving—
So whatever\'s in that quarry, it\'s the same thing that was in the tide caves.
The scarecrows in Thistledown were stuffed with purple dust — like the crystal in the tide caves. Tam\'s gang sold it. Whatever is in that quarry, it\'s the same thing.
Oi! Quarry\'s closed. Toll\'s your boots, your purse and your dignity.
And the archer on the ridge says the rest. Back, Wren.
Not this way. Somebody in Thistledown must know another way up.
Right. Bethan\'s herb path. Behind the hedge, east end of the fields.
A dense hawthorn hedge. Someone has woven it tight here, on purpose. You can smell rosemary and mint behind it.
"Weeps" was last week. This week it\'s "the red sky sleeps."
"The red sky sleeps." Remember that. Or I will. I\'ll remember it for you.
Nib and Gorse were arguing about this. Sleeps, not weeps.
Right you are. Go on, then. ...Here, I don\'t know your faces—
...He _is_, though. Nobody ever says it. Go on through. Wait, I don\'t know your faces—
Oh! Welcome! Mind the archers, they\'re twitchy. Hearth\'s warm up top.
Well, well, _well_. Somebody got past Hollis. Somebody always gets past Hollis.
Let\'s see. A Dawnguard squire. A hedge-witch. A redheaded fishwife with a sword she don\'t know how to hold. And—
—and _there_ she is. Black hair. Pale as milk.
Sweetheart, you are worth more silver than this whole valley.

You\'ll have to go through me.

Alright! Alright. Yield. I yield. Mercy. Uncle. All the good words.
